summary: Madagascar admits every nationality with a tourist visa issued on arrival or online in advance — 15-, 30- and 60-day tiers priced by length of stay — making entry straightforward for all passports.

primarySources.name: eVisa Madagascar — official travel authorisation portal (linked as “Visa pour Madagascar” by the Ministry of Tourism)

defaultSource.name: eVisa Madagascar — official travel authorisation portal (home: eligibility, visa on arrival, 60-day maximum)

conflict.name: UK FCDO — Madagascar entry requirements
conflict.states: UK visitors can stay up to 15 days without a visa, paying a EUR 10 administration fee on arrival

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from your arrival date in Madagascar, with at least two blank pages.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required only if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. There is no yellow fever in Madagascar itself.

onwardTicket.text: Be ready to show onward or return tickets on arrival, according to the UK FCDO. The eVisa portal itself does not state the rule.

declarations.name: Health declaration form and screening (Ebola measures)
declarations.text: Because of the Ebola outbreak, all travellers must complete a health declaration form, declare any travel through an Ebola-affected country in the previous 21 days, and undergo health screening on arrival. If you have been in or transited through an affected country in the last 21 days you may be refused entry unless exempt (nationals, residents, work or student visa holders, diplomats and international-organisation or NGO staff), and exempt travellers must complete a 21-day quarantine at an approved location at their own cost.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Madagascar travel advice: entry requirements

currencyLimits.text: Foreign cash or travellers' cheques worth EUR 7,500 or more must be declared on arrival — keep the certified declaration, or the money can be seized when you leave. You may bring in up to 400,000 Malagasy ariary.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Madagascar travel advice: entry requirements

conflict.name: Government of Canada — Travel advice and advisories for Madagascar
conflict.states: You must declare foreign currency in excess of 10,000 euros on arrival.

notes: The UK FCDO says it is illegal to take any food, including fruit, into Madagascar. On leaving, after declaring and showing receipts, you may take out up to 2 kg of vanilla and up to 1 kg of pepper or cloves; other plant and animal products need permission.
The UK FCDO says it is illegal to collect, buy or export protected animals, plants or products made from them, including items made of rosewood.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says Madagascar has a cash-based economy: some credit cards are accepted at major hotels, some restaurants and shops, and cash can be withdrawn from a limited number of ATMs in Antananarivo. Euros are widely accepted and US dollars sometimes; ariary may not be taken out of the country.

safety.text: The UK FCDO says robberies and thefts are commonplace throughout Madagascar and that there have been violent robberies and assaults on isolated beaches, even in daytime. It advises avoiding political demonstrations and large gatherings, not walking alone in city centres or poorly lit areas after dark, and using pre-booked taxis or hotel transport.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Madagascar travel advice: safety and security

bestTimeToVisit.text: No official seasonal guidance for visitors. The UK FCDO says the cyclone season normally runs from November to April, with coastal areas particularly at risk, and that in the December–April rainy season many secondary roads are impassable except by 4-wheel-drive.

idp.text: Madagascar is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Madagascar is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Madagascar yet.

tips.text: The UK FCDO says the cyclone season normally runs from November to April, with coastal areas particularly at risk; storms can cut access to remote parts of the country and contaminate water supplies. Monitor forecasts and allow slack in your plans.

Canada's travel advice says the military took over on 14 October 2025 after large-scale demonstrations and announced a two-year transition. Demonstrations are frequent and can turn violent: avoid them and large gatherings, and follow local news.

Canada's travel advice says cash can be withdrawn from only a limited number of ATMs in Antananarivo and that some banks will not convert ariary back into hard currency, so plan your cash before leaving the capital.

The UK FCDO says road conditions vary greatly and are often poor, advises against driving at night, and says many secondary roads are impassable except by 4-wheel-drive in the December–April rainy season. It also warns of armed robberies on main roads, particularly at night.

Canada's travel advice says there is a risk of malaria in certain areas and at certain times of year, and that antimalarial medication may be recommended depending on your itinerary — see a health professional before you travel and use insect repellent.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Madagascar?
faq.answer: Yes, but it is easy: every nationality can obtain a tourist visa, either on arrival at the airport or online in advance at evisamada-mg.com. Visas come in 15-, 30- and 60-day versions, with the fee depending on length of stay.

faq.question: How much does the Madagascar visa cost?
faq.answer: The official eVisa portal lists EUR 30 (USD 35) for up to 15 days, EUR 35 (USD 41) for 16–30 days and EUR 40 (USD 47) for 31–60 days. Confirm the current amounts on the eVisa portal before travel.

faq.question: Should I get the eVisa or a visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Both lead to the same tourist visa. Applying at evisamada-mg.com before travel saves queueing after a long flight, while the visa on arrival remains available to all nationalities at international airports — if you choose it, carry the fee in cash.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Madagascar?
faq.answer: Tourist stays can generally be extended in-country up to a maximum of around 90 days in total, handled by the Ministry of the Interior in Antananarivo. Start well before your visa expires and confirm the current procedure locally — requirements change.

faq.question: Is Madagascar safe to visit?
faq.answer: Take care. Canada's travel advice says petty crime is common throughout the country, that violent crime is reported in all regions, and that armed gangs have assaulted tourists in isolated areas such as beaches and national parks. Demonstrations are frequent and can turn violent, and the UK FCDO says the cyclone season normally runs from November to April.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Madagascar?
faq.answer: No official source we could read gives seasonal guidance for visitors. The UK FCDO says the cyclone season normally runs from November to April and that many secondary roads are impassable except by 4-wheel-drive in the December–April rainy season.
